01 Reading · The Vendor Who Remembered My Name 7 min read
By Yuki Tanaka · Travel Essayist · Kyoto & London
Listen

Traveling alone, I quickly learned to rely on the kindness of strangers — the elderly woman at the market who slipped an extra plum into my bag, the taxi driver who waited for me outside the station without complaint. Nobody at home believed in my ability to manage two months alone in a country whose language I barely spoke. I was afraid of getting lost, worried about running out of money, and secretly proud of myself for buying the plane ticket at all.

By the third week, the market felt nothing like home — different from the quiet supermarkets I was used to, loud and specific and warm. There was a fish vendor, a man everyone seemed to depend on for the freshest catch, who somehow remembered my name after a single conversation. I apologized for my terrible pronunciation every time I ordered, and every time he laughed and corrected me anyway.

"He never asked what I was looking for. He simply gave me something to look forward to."

I hadn't expected to succeed in making a single local friend, let alone several. I was surprised at how quickly the city stopped feeling foreign. The vendor's daughter, who was studying to become a teacher, was interested in practicing her English, and we began meeting for tea every Sunday — both of us satisfied with a friendship built on nothing more than a shared market stall and imperfect grammar on both sides.

Looking back, I'm grateful to that vendor more than almost anyone else on the trip. He never asked what I was looking for. He simply gave me something to look forward to, every single week, in a language I was only just beginning to understand.

Glossary
vendor · 売り子 · vendedor(a)
plum · 梅 · ameixa
catch (noun) · 漁獲 · pesca do dia
market stall · 屋台・露店 · barraca de mercado
slip (verb) · そっと入れる · colocar discretamente
let alone · まして〜ない · muito menos, quanto mais
Spot the Preposition
1.
Find one verb + preposition combination used for feelings of trust. rely on / depend on / believe in
2.
Find one adjective + preposition combination describing an emotion. afraid of / worried about / proud of / surprised at
3.
What does Yuki say she was surprised at? How quickly the city stopped feeling foreign.
02 Grammar Focus · Verb + Preposition explanation + 8 items
PrepositionVerbsExample
ONdepend, rely"You can always depend on / rely on your family in a crisis."
INbelieve, succeed"She believes in hard work, and it helped her succeed in the exam."
FORapologize, apply, wait"I apologized for being late, then waited for the bus, then applied for the job online."
ABOUTworry, care"Don't worry about the weather — we both care about having fun more than staying dry."
WITHagree, deal"I agree with your plan, but you'll have to deal with your brother's complaints."
Tradução · Verb + Preposition
depend on · 頼る・依存する · depender de
rely on · 頼る・当てにする · contar com
believe in · 信じる · acreditar em
succeed in · 成功する · ter sucesso em / conseguir
apologize for · 謝る · pedir desculpas por
apply for · 応募する · candidatar-se a
wait for · 待つ · esperar por
worry about · 心配する · preocupar-se com
care about · 気にかける · importar-se com
agree with · 同意する · concordar com
deal with · 対処する · lidar com
look forward to · 楽しみにする · estar ansioso por
Real Talk These combinations don't follow a logical rule — the preposition is simply part of the verb's identity, the way a person's name comes with a surname. Depend on is a single unit of meaning, not "depend" plus a preposition you choose freely. The only real strategy is repetition: read them, hear them, and notice them in context until they feel automatic — the same way look forward to is always followed by a noun or -ing form, never a bare infinitive ("I look forward to see you" is a very common mistake — it should be "seeing").
つまり: これらの組み合わせには論理的なルールはなく、前置詞は動詞のアイデンティティの一部です。唯一の戦略は繰り返しです — 文脈の中で読んで、聞いて、自然に身につくまで気づき続けること。"look forward to" の後は常に名詞か -ing 形（"look forward to seeing you"）で、原形不定詞ではありません。

Complete each sentence with the correct preposition.

1.
I'm really looking forward to seeing the autumn leaves this year.
2.
The whole village depends on tourism during the summer months.
3.
She apologized for the delay and offered us a free drink.
4.
I don't fully agree with the new check-in policy.
5.
He applied for a job at the ryokan and started the following month.
6.
Please don't worry about the extra luggage — we have plenty of space.
7.
After years of practice, she finally succeeded in opening her own tea shop.
8.
I'll deal with the reservation — you can relax and enjoy the view.
03 Grammar Focus · Adjective + Preposition explanation + 8 items
PrepositionAdjectivesExample
INinterested"She's interested in Japanese pottery."
OFafraid, proud, aware"He's not afraid of spiders, and he's proud of it — though not always aware of how loudly he says so."
ABOUTworried"I'm worried about missing the last train."
FORfamous, responsible"This town is famous for its hot springs, and the mayor is responsible for protecting them."
TOsimilar"This ryokan is similar to the one we stayed at last year."
FROMdifferent"City life is very different from village life."
WITHsatisfied"We were satisfied with the service."
Tradução · Adjective + Preposition
interested in · 興味がある · interessado em
afraid of · 怖がる · com medo de
proud of · 誇りに思う · orgulhoso de
aware of · 気づいている · ciente de
worried about · 心配している · preocupado com
famous for · 〜で有名 · famoso por
responsible for · 〜に責任がある · responsável por
similar to · 〜に似ている · parecido com
different from · 〜と違う · diferente de
satisfied with · 満足している · satisfeito com
surprised at · 驚いている · surpreso com
good at · 〜が得意 · bom em
Real Talk Same idea as verb + preposition, but watch two famous traps. First: married takes to, not "with" ("married to a doctor," never "married with"). Second: different traditionally takes from in careful writing, though you'll hear "different to" in British English and "different than" in American English — from is always safe and correct everywhere.
つまり: 動詞+前置詞と同じ考え方ですが、2つの有名な罠に注意 — "married" は "with" ではなく必ず "to"。"different" は正式には "from" ですが、イギリス英語では "different to"、アメリカ英語では "different than" も聞かれます。"from" はどこでも常に正解です。

Complete each sentence with the correct preposition.

1.
I've always been interested in the history of tea ceremonies.
2.
This dish is very different from anything I've tried before.
3.
He's genuinely afraid of flying, even after all these years.
4.
This region is famous for its cherry blossoms in spring.
5.
We were very satisfied with the room, even though it was small.
6.
I'm a little worried about the typhoon reaching the coast this weekend.
7.
She's always been good at reading maps, even without her phone.
8.

04 Grammar Focus · Questions Ending in a Preposition engine + 8 items

You already know this move from passive voice — the preposition gets left behind ("stranded") at the end of the question. Now we'll use the same skill with dependent prepositions to ask about opinions, feelings, and habits.

1
Find the preposition partner. Locate the verb or adjective and its fixed preposition in the statement.
"She is interested in modern art." → interested IN
2
Turn the object into a question word. A thing becomes what; a person becomes who. Move it to the front.
"modern art" → What
3
Add the question form, and strand the preposition at the end. Don't drag it to the front — that's only for very formal writing ("In what is she interested?" sounds stiff and old-fashioned).
"What is she interested in?"
Real Talk A second example, this time with a verb: "He depends on his sister." Step 1: depends ON. Step 2: "his sister" → who. Step 3: bring in the auxiliary does and strand the preposition: "Who does he depend on?" Notice the verb drops back to its base form (depends → depend) once does appears — same rule as any other present simple question.
つまり: 動詞の例 — "He depends on his sister." ステップ1: depends ON。ステップ2: "his sister" → who。ステップ3: 助動詞 does を加え、前置詞を最後に残す: "Who does he depend on?"。does が出てきたら動詞は原形に戻ります（depends → depend）。

Transform each statement into a question ending in a preposition. The underlined part is what you're asking about.

1.
She is worried about the exam results. → What is she worried about?
2.
He relies on his eldest daughter. → Who does he rely on?
3.
The plan is similar to last year's itinerary. → What is the plan similar to?
4.
They are proud of their grandson. → Who are they proud of?
5.
She applied for a teaching position. → What did she apply for?
6.
He's responsible for the whole kitchen. → What is he responsible for?
7.
The company is dealing with a difficult supplier. → Who is the company dealing with?
8.
You're most afraid of something specific. → What are you most afraid of?
05 Mixed Practice · Prepositions & Questions 12 items

Items 1–8 need the missing preposition. Items 9–12 ask you to turn a statement into a question ending in a preposition.

1.
This tea is famous for its bitterness — locals say it's an acquired taste.
2.
I'm aware of the rules, but the sign was still hard to find.
3.
She succeeded in convincing the whole family to travel together this year.
4.
He's not satisfied with the new schedule — too many early mornings.
5.
We're really looking forward to the festival next weekend.
6.
The whole staff depends on the head chef's schedule.
7.
I was surprised at how empty the shrine was on a Sunday.
8.
He apologized for forgetting the reservation.
9.
She's afraid of heights. → What is she afraid of?
10.
He agrees with his business partner. → Who does he agree with?
11.
The festival is similar to a harvest celebration. → What is the festival similar to?
12.
They're grateful to the rescue team. → Who are they grateful to?
06 Scenario Corner · Ask & Answer 8 prompts

For each prompt, first write the question ending in a preposition, then answer it about your own life. If you're practicing with your teacher, ask each other out loud.

01
Ask about something a person is interested in.
Q: "What are you interested in these days?" A: "Honestly, I've been interested in local pottery — I keep finding small shops I didn't know existed."
02
Ask who someone relies on the most.
Q: "Who do you rely on the most when you travel?" A: "I rely on my sister — she's the one who actually reads the map."
03
Ask what someone is afraid of.
Q: "What are you most afraid of when traveling alone?" A: "I'm afraid of missing the last train and having nowhere to stay."
04
Ask what someone is proud of.
Q: "What are you most proud of from the last year?" A: "I'm proud of finally planning a trip entirely by myself."
05
Ask what a place or thing is famous for.
Q: "What is your hometown famous for?" A: "It's famous for its hot springs and a very old wooden bridge."
06
Ask who someone is grateful to, and why.
Q: "Who are you most grateful to from your travels?" A: "I'm grateful to a stranger who walked me to the station in the rain."
07
Ask what someone is worried about right now.
Q: "What are you worried about right now?" A: "I'm worried about the typhoon delaying my flight home."
08 · YOUR OWN QUESTIONS
Write two of your own questions using different dependent prepositions from today's lesson — then ask a friend or your teacher.
07 Closing · Takeaways
  • Verb + preposition: depend on, rely on, believe in, succeed in, apologize for, apply for, wait for, worry about, care about, agree with, deal with, look forward to.
  • Adjective + preposition: interested in, afraid of, proud of, aware of, worried about, famous for, responsible for, similar to, different from, satisfied with, surprised at, good at.
  • Questions ending in a preposition: find the preposition partner → turn the object into what/who → strand the preposition at the end. "Who does he depend on?" not "On whom does he depend?"
  • There's no shortcut for memorizing which preposition goes with which word — only repetition. Every time you notice one "in the wild," it's worth pausing on.
